title: Violin Concerto in E minor
hook: The violin sings from the second bar, and the three movements run on without a pause.

painting.title: The Balcony Room
painting.pairingNote: A breeze lifts a thin curtain and sunlight pours into an empty room in Berlin, Mendelssohn’s home city, painted the year the concerto was first played; the music has the same lightness and fresh air.

facts: Mendelssohn wrote it for Ferdinand David, the leader of his orchestra in Leipzig, the Gewandhaus. They had been born a year apart in the same house in Hamburg. In July 1838 Mendelssohn wrote to him that a concerto in E minor was running through his head and that its beginning gave him no peace.
It took six years. The score is dated 16 September 1844, and all along Mendelssohn kept asking David how to make the solo part work on the violin.
David played the premiere in Leipzig on 13 March 1845. Mendelssohn was ill, so the Danish composer Niels Gade conducted.

It broke three habits. The violin enters almost at once, with no long orchestral introduction. The [[cadenza|cadenza]] is written out by the composer and comes in the middle of the first movement, not near the end. And the three movements are joined without pauses, [[attacca|attacca]], so nobody applauds between them.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a passionate, urgent song (I), a calm song without words (II), a light, sparkling dance after a fanfare (III).

movements.heading: Allegro molto appassionato
movements.summary: After a bar and a half of soft, nervous strings, the violin starts singing a passionate melody high up. It is a movement in [[sonata-form|sonata form]], urgent and restless, with one moment of complete calm: a quiet hymn in the woodwinds over a single low note from the violin.

mainIdeas.name: The opening melody
mainIdeas.description: long, yearning and high, in E minor, on the solo violin over murmuring strings.

mainIdeas.name: The hymn
mainIdeas.description: a quiet, slow tune in G major for clarinets and flutes, while the violin holds its lowest note underneath.

mainIdeas.name: The bouncing arpeggios
mainIdeas.description: quick chords bounced across all four strings of the violin, the sound that opens the recapitulation.

notice: Listen for the low note under the woodwind hymn (≈ 3:15). The violin plays just one note for a long time, while others have the tune.
In the cadenza, wait for the bouncing chords. They do not stop when the orchestra comes back. The soloist is suddenly the accompanist.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Mutter was 17. Karajan and the Berlin Philharmonic take broad tempos, so the first movement lasts almost fourteen minutes. Heifetz, in the alternative recording, plays it in eleven.

movements.heading: Andante
movements.summary: A slow movement that sounds like one of Mendelssohn’s *Songs without Words*. The violin sings a long, simple melody over a gentle, rocking accompaniment. In the middle the music darkens and grows anxious, then the melody comes back.

mainIdeas.name: The song
mainIdeas.description: a long, calm melody in C major, sung by the violin in its middle register.

mainIdeas.name: The middle section
mainIdeas.description: a darker, troubled passage in the minor, with trembling strings.

stops.hear: The bassoon’s held note slides up, and the orchestra plays a short, gentle introduction
stops.happening: The link from movement I, into C major

stops.hear: The violin begins a long, simple, singing melody over a soft, rocking accompaniment
stops.happening: The main melody

stops.hear: Darker and more agitated; the strings tremble, and the violin plays two lines at once
stops.happening: The middle section, in A minor, with [[tremolo|tremolo]] strings and violin [[double-stop|double stop]]s

stops.hear: The calm, singing melody returns
stops.happening: The main melody again

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The violin’s line fades away quietly, ending in C major
stops.happening: The close

notice: In the middle section, the violin plays two notes at once, a melody and its own accompaniment. Listen for the second, lower line.

movements.heading: Allegretto non troppo – Allegro molto vivace
movements.tempo: Allegretto non troppo – Allegro molto vivace
movements.summary: A short, wistful bridge, then a fanfare, and the finale takes off: quick, light and sparkling, like Mendelssohn’s fairy music for *A Midsummer Night’s Dream*. The violin skips and flickers, and the orchestra answers with a bold march.

mainIdeas.name: The bridge
mainIdeas.description: a few bars of quiet, wistful music for the violin and strings, still in the minor.

mainIdeas.name: The fanfare
mainIdeas.description: trumpets, horns and timpani announce the finale.

mainIdeas.name: The main theme
mainIdeas.description: quick, light, staccato notes on the violin, in a bright E major.

mainIdeas.name: The march
mainIdeas.description: a bold, strong tune for the orchestra.

stops.hear: Trumpets, horns and drums sound a fanfare; the violin answers with quick, rising flourishes
stops.happening: The finale begins, *Allegro molto vivace*

stops.hear: A quick, light, skipping tune on the violin, with crisp, short notes in the orchestra

notice: At ≈ 3:10 two tunes play at once: a slow one on the violin, a quick one underneath. Try to follow both.

threads.title: No pauses
threads.body: A held bassoon note links the first two movements, and a short bridge links the second to the third. The whole concerto is meant to be heard in one sweep.

threads.title: The soloist from the start
threads.body: The violin enters in the second bar and hardly ever stops. There is no long wait while the orchestra plays the themes first.

threads.title: A friend’s advice
threads.body: Mendelssohn was a pianist and conductor; Ferdinand David, a violinist, helped him shape the solo part over six years.

threads.title: Lightness
threads.body: Even the passionate first movement moves quickly, and the finale flickers like his fairy music. Little in it is heavy.
